# From Safety Evaluations to Policy Action

**How should European policymakers use frontier AI safety evaluations when deciding whether additional oversight or safeguards are warranted?**

Safety evaluations can reveal dangerous AI capabilities, but they **do not tell us everything about real-world risks**. This project explores how policymakers can interpret these results, understand their limitations, and use them to make better decisions.

::: {.intro-grid}
::: {.intro-label}
### THE POLICY PROBLEM
:::
::: {.intro-copy}
_An evaluation result is evidence about a model under specified conditions - not a guarantee of safety in deployment._

Public policy needs a defensible way to move from **what was tested**, to **what the evidence supports**, to **what an authority might do next**. The proposed contribution is a concise policy analysis of that translation, not a new benchmark, certification system, or claim that existing EU rules lack evaluation requirements.
:::
:::

## Policy case: Evaluating dangerous cyber capabilities {#case-study}

::: {.section-subtitle}
**Hypothetical illustration, not a real model assessment.** Consider a frontier model whose developer reports that it passed internal safety evaluations relating to potentially dangerous cyber capabilities. How useful is that statement to an authority considering systemic risks?
:::

::: {.platform-panel}
<div class="platform-head">
  <div class="platform-eyebrow">ILLUSTRATIVE CLAIM</div>
  <h3>“Our frontier AI model passed its safety evaluations.”</h3>
  <p>What would an EU decision-maker need to know before relying on that claim?</p>
</div>
<div class="platform-branches" aria-label="Three stages of interpreting frontier AI safety evidence">
  <div class="platform-branch">
<span class="branch-number">01 · EVIDENCE</span>
<strong>What was actually tested?</strong>
<span>Which cyber-related capabilities were evaluated? Were tests adversarial and independently scrutinized? What tasks, access, safeguards, and model versions were covered? What failures or limits were disclosed?</span>
<em>“Passed” is not meaningful without a documented scope and criteria.</em>
  </div>
  <div class="platform-branch">
<span class="branch-number">02 · INFERENCE</span>
<strong>What can we conclude?</strong>
<span>How closely do test conditions resemble plausible misuse or deployment scenarios? Could access to tools, user adaptation, or later model changes alter the risk? Which uncertainties remain?</span>
<em>Capability findings do not directly quantify real-world likelihood or harm.</em>
  </div>
  <div class="platform-branch">
<span class="branch-number">03 · POLICY</span>
<strong>What action is justified?</strong>
<span>Depending on the evidence, should the relevant authority seek further documentation, examine mitigation measures, request additional evaluation, or consider other oversight steps within its legal powers?</span>
<em>Responses should reflect risk, uncertainty, proportionality, and legal authority.</em>
  </div>
</div>
:::

<br>

**Why this matters in Europe:** 

- The [EU AI Act, Article 55](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-55), already requires providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk to evaluate their models, assess and mitigate risks, report serious incidents, and ensure appropriate cybersecurity protection.

But an important question remains: **How can evidence from AI safety evaluations better support the implementation and supervision of these requirements?**

**Potential policy output:**

- A short policy brief examining what current safety evaluations reveal, what information may be missing, and how European policymakers could use this evidence to improve oversight.

## A framework for policy-relevant evidence {#questions}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Three questions connect AI safety evidence to accountable European governance. The framework is deliberately decision-oriented rather than a comprehensive technical evaluation methodology.
:::

::: {.workflow aria-label="Three questions for policy-relevant safety evidence"}
::: {.step}
<div class="step-top"><span class="step-number">01</span><span class="step-tag">EVIDENCE QUALITY</span></div>
<h3>Can we assess the evaluation claim?</h3>
<p>Examine test scope, methods, provenance, independence, disclosed limitations, and whether a claim is supported by the underlying evidence.</p>
<div class="step-prompt">Scope · Transparency · Independence · Reproducibility</div>
:::
<div class="connector" aria-hidden="true">↓</div>
::: {.step}
<div class="step-top"><span class="step-number">02</span><span class="step-tag">RISK INTERPRETATION</span></div>
<h3>What does the result imply about risk?</h3>
<p>Distinguish measured capabilities from misuse scenarios and broader systemic risk. Consider external validity, uncertainty, protective measures, and missing information.</p>
<div class="step-prompt">Capability vs. risk · Generalizability · Uncertainty</div>
:::
<div class="connector" aria-hidden="true">↓</div>
::: {.step .step-final}
<div class="step-top"><span class="step-number">03</span><span class="step-tag">POLICY RESPONSE</span></div>
<h3>What should authorities consider doing?</h3>
<p>Identify feasible reporting improvements, review questions, and possible follow-up measures, distinguishing existing legal requirements from new policy proposals.</p>
<div class="step-prompt">Institutional authority · Proportionality · Accountability</div>
:::
:::

## Proposed approach {#workflow}

::: {.section-subtitle}
A bounded desk-based policy project using public sources. Any empirical comparison would depend on available, sufficiently comparable material.
:::

::: {.output-grid}
::: {.output-card}
<div class="output-index">STEP 01</div>
<h3>Map existing duties</h3>
<p>Summarize relevant EU requirements and guidance for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, focusing on evaluation, risk management, and oversight.</p>
:::
::: {.output-card}
<div class="output-index">STEP 02</div>
<h3>Review public evidence</h3>
<p>Compare a small, clearly selected set of public safety evaluation documents. Record what is reported, what remains unknown, and which claims can be supported.</p>
:::
::: {.output-card}
<div class="output-index">STEP 03</div>
<h3>Develop policy options</h3>
<p>Identify practical improvements to decision-relevant reporting or scrutiny; distinguish feasible proposals from legal duties and note trade-offs.</p>
:::
:::

::: {.integrity-note}
<div class="note-symbol" aria-hidden="true">↗</div>
<div>
<strong>Scope and research integrity</strong>

This is a proposed policy exercise. No model testing, independent audit, interviews, original data collection, or empirical validation has been completed. A cyber-capability test does not by itself establish the probability of harm. Examples are hypothetical; recommendations would require source review and attention to confidentiality, legal powers, and institutional feasibility.
</div>
:::

## Potential Policy Contribution: a European policy brief {#output}

::: {.intro-grid}
::: {.intro-label}
### PROPOSED DELIVERABLE
:::
::: {.intro-copy}
**Working title:** _Making Frontier AI Safety Evaluations Decision-Useful for European Policymakers_

A concise policy brief would examine how public reporting on frontier AI evaluations can better support oversight of models with potential systemic risks. It would explain a specific evidence-to-decision gap, assess relevant European institutional and legal context, and propose a limited number of actionable improvements-with trade-offs and uncertainties made explicit.

A small **evidence matrix** could support the brief by tracing each documented claim to its source, limitations, and policy relevance. The brief - not a software platform or a completed research study - would be the principal proposed output.
:::
:::
